semantic_correction.stem: A medically stable client with chronic heart failure asks why the health care team recommends cardiac rehabilitation. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: It combines exercise training with risk-factor management and can improve functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and quality of life in appropriate stable heart failure.
options.B: It is designed mainly for recovery after myocardial infarction, so stable heart failure is not a usual indication unless a recent coronary event has also occurred.
options.C: It focuses on education and risk-factor review, while exercise training is generally avoided in stable heart failure because it can worsen functional capacity.
options.D: It can replace guideline-directed heart-failure medications after exercise tolerance improves because rehabilitation becomes the main treatment once the program begins.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. The 2024 AHA/AACVPR scientific statement identifies stable heart failure as an indication for cardiac rehabilitation and describes cardiac rehabilitation as a medically supervised secondary-prevention program that includes exercise training, risk-factor management, nutrition, psychosocial care, and physical-activity counseling. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart-failure guideline states that cardiac rehabilitation can improve functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and health-related quality of life in patients with heart failure who are able to participate. B is incorrect because stable heart failure itself is an accepted indication for cardiac rehabilitation. C is incorrect because exercise training is a core component and is recommended for appropriate patients with heart failure. D is incorrect because cardiac rehabilitation complements rather than replaces guideline-directed heart-failure therapy.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain that cardiac rehabilitation is an evidence-based secondary-prevention strategy for appropriate stable heart-failure clients that combines exercise and risk-factor management and improves functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and quality of life without replacing medical therapy.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American Heart Association/American Association of Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Rehabilitation (AHA/AACVPR); American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America (AHA/ACC/HFSA)

semantic_correction.source_locator: Core Components of Cardiac Rehabilitation Programs: 2024 Update — Top Things to Know, item 1: cardiac rehabilitation is indicated for a broad cardiovascular population including stable heart failure; items 3–4 and 10: core components include prescribed exercise, cardiovascular risk-factor modification, psychosocial assessment, nutritional counseling, physical-activity counseling, and medically supervised secondary prevention. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline — Section 7.1.3, Management of Stage C HF: Activity, Exercise Prescription, and Cardiac Rehabilitation: exercise training is recommended for patients with HF who can participate to improve functional status, exercise performance, and quality of life; cardiac rehabilitation can be useful to improve functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and health-related quality of life.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the uniquely-long correct-answer cue, eliminated an unnecessary heart-failure hospitalization claim, and rebuilt all four options as balanced cardiac-rehabilitation explanations anchored to current AHA/AACVPR and AHA/ACC/HFSA guidance.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests why cardiac rehabilitation is used in stable heart failure, with one clearly best answer and no unsupported hospitalization or mortality claim.

option_audit.A: Correct. Stable heart failure is an accepted indication, and the cited HF guideline directly supports improvements in functional capacity, exercise tolerance, and health-related quality of life.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Cardiac rehabilitation is not limited to post-myocardial-infarction care; the 2024 AHA/AACVPR statement explicitly includes stable heart failure among indications.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Exercise training is a core component of cardiac rehabilitation and is recommended for heart-failure patients who are able to participate.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Cardiac rehabilitation is a secondary-prevention adjunct and does not replace guideline-directed heart-failure medications.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone accurately describes both the indication and supported benefits of cardiac rehabilitation in stable heart failure; B excludes a recognized indication, C reverses the exercise recommendation, and D falsely substitutes rehabilitation for medical therapy.
cueing_check: The choices are closely balanced in length (A 171, B 163, C 159, D 168 characters), use parallel explanations, and no option is uniquely detailed or structurally privileged enough to reveal the correct answer.
